source.title: Learning a Single Neuron with Gradient Methods

record.tranche_reason: Analyzes whether standard gradient methods can learn a single neuron, using different model and loss settings from the claim’s benchmark classification versions.
record.gate_note: Results are for a single neuron trained on a population squared-loss objective, not benchmark classification error. Cited results from other work are excluded. Rows record this study’s own theorems and its reported gradient-descent experiment.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes convergence of a single neuron on population squared loss. Its results do not test any stated version: there are no benchmark convolutional classifiers, width comparisons, depth comparisons, signal-preserving initialization comparisons, stability-threshold dynamics, or normalization comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the authors establish constant-probability convergence under mild distribution and activation assumptions, high-probability ReLU gradient-flow convergence for spherical inputs, and constructed optimization failures. Their shifted-Gaussian experiment challenges monotonic-angle proof strategies while still converging; general high-probability convergence remains open.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes gradient methods for a single neuron on population squared loss, rather than large benchmark classifiers trained for classification error.
record.method_sensitivity: The guarantees depend on distributional assumptions, activation assumptions, initialization region, and (for SGD) learning-rate and iteration bounds. The angle behavior in the reported experiment varies over trajectory and is non-monotonic.

fits_no_version.finding: For any product initialization, a bounded input distribution and target can be constructed such that gradient flow, GD, and SGD remain at least 1/(8d) above optimal population loss with probability at least 1 − exp(−d/4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-ReLU-neuron optimization can fail persistently under unfavorable input distributions, even in a realizable setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Under spread-distribution and activation assumptions, qualifying initializations yield convergence guarantees; suitable small Gaussian initialization gives success probability close to one-half. Spherical inputs permit an exponentially high probability guarantee for ReLU gradient flow with N(0, I/d) initialization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Single-neuron population-loss convergence depends on distribution, activation, initialization, and step-size conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: For the shifted-Gaussian experiment, GD eventually reaches the global minimum despite a non-monotonic angle to the target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Successful single-ReLU-neuron optimization need not monotonically decrease the angle to the target.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Conference on Computational Learning Theory (COLT)
record.problems: The positive convergence results require explicit assumptions and apply to a single-neuron population-loss setting. The non-monotonic-angle evidence is an empirical R² example with three initializations; the paper does not provide numerical uncertainty for it.

untested.parts: All: convolutional-network training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including random labels and the stated training-recipe qualifications.
All: spurious-minimum frequency as teacher and student widths grow, and the effect of adding student neurons.
All: depth-related training degradation, residual shortcuts, and the stated deep-network initialization exceptions.
All: activation-matched signal and gradient preservation, training speed and depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization.
All: recovery above initial stability thresholds, curvature dynamics, edge-of-stability training, and divergence.
All: batch-normalization speed and learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6 because their measures match no version. This does not dispute the reported single-neuron results. No additional version-relevant results require missing rows.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification error, convolutional networks, corrupted or random labels, model size, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious minima frequency, and student width relative to teacher width.
Depth, batch normalization, identity shortcuts, ImageNet/CIFAR-10 training error, and the stated special initialization settings.
Comparisons of activation-matched, Gaussian, or orthogonal initializations; training speed across depth; and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning rates above a stability threshold, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and divergence.
Batch normalization’s effect on speed or learning-rate tolerance, and Fixup residual-network comparisons.

rows.subject: single ReLU neuron
rows.operation_detail: Gradient descent on the population objective with constant step size η = 10⁻³.
rows.measure: Angle between learned vector and target over iterations
rows.value: Angle is initially increasing rather than decreasing; algorithm eventually reaches global minimum w = v.
rows.note: The three initializations are reported together for the figure; the prose describes the angle as non-monotonic and says it appears to attain every value in (0, π].
rows.check: Non-monotonic angle and eventual convergence measure no claim version. The reported partial state must not imply partial optimization success: the authors explicitly report eventual convergence to the global minimum.
